source.title: Self-directed speech affects visual search performance

confidence_rationale: This is the canonical direct test of MECH-383's exact claim: producing a self-directed label ('saying the target name aloud') temporarily improves visual SEARCH for that target -- a perceptual-control intervention, not a post-perceptual report. The design is causal (within-subject manipulation of speaking vs not speaking the target name) and the effect is graded by name-target association strength, which matches MECH-383's framing of labels as tunable top-down signals. Confidence held below 0.8 because the manipulation is overt natural-language speech in humans and the boundary condition (speaking HURTS when the label mismatches the target) shows the control input is not free -- both relevant transfer caveats for a non-linguistic REE substrate.
failure_signatures: The facilitation reverses to IMPAIRMENT as the discrepancy between the spoken name and the visual target grows -- a mis-specified label actively degrades search, so a label-as-control input in REE would need accurate label generation to be net-beneficial (no free lunch).

The effect is on visual SEARCH (finding a known target among distractors), which is template-matching/attentional, not on detecting genuinely novel or unexpected cues -- so the paper supports the 'bias toward label-relevant cues' reading of MECH-383 more strongly than the 'novelty-gradient toward unexplained change' reading.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Saying a target object's name aloud before/during visual search facilitates finding it (faster, more accurate), particularly when the name-to-object association is strong; as the name-target discrepancy increases, speaking begins to impair search. Verbal labels can therefore temporarily change ongoing perceptual processing -- hearing 'chair' makes the visual system a better 'chair detector' (label-feedback hypothesis).
mapping.ree_translation: Direct grounding for MECH-383: a self-directed label ('food-gradient', 'danger-gradient', 'blocked-goal') is a top-down tuning signal that biases perceptual search toward label-relevant cues, not merely a description appended after perception. The graded, association-dependent effect maps onto MECH-383's framing of labels as control INPUTS to the precision-routing plane (ARC-005, MECH-251/261), and the impairment-on-mismatch shows the input has real, sign-dependent authority over perception.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The label here is overt natural-language speech in humans; REE has no language and would generate labels as internal control tokens. The demonstrated effect is on template-guided SEARCH for a known target, not on open-ended novelty detection -- so it grounds the cue-biasing half of MECH-383 better than the unexplained-change-detection half.
mapping.source_context: Human behavioural psychophysics; within-subject visual-search task with a speak-the-name manipulation; n in the standard cognitive-psychology range.

confidence_components.notes: Well-designed causal within-subject behavioural study, widely cited as the canonical self-directed-speech-and-search result; source quality good. Mapping fidelity high -- the paper tests almost exactly what MECH-383 asserts. Transfer risk elevated by the natural-language modality and the search-vs-novelty scope limit.
